chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: A slow driver prevents you from proceeding quickly. What is right?

options.text: You follow him until there is a possibility to overtake
You flash your headlights to make him drive faster
You close up to him in order to shorten the overtaking distance

correct_answers.text: You follow him until there is a possibility to overtake

comment: Never start a risky overtaking maneuver or force your frontman to speed up with your flash light. Keep the necessary safety distance and wait for a convenient opportunity for safe overtaking.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: What makes a good driver?

options.text: He treats others like partners, drives calmly and cooly and refrains from showing that he is superior
He uses every possibility to overtake, give the slip to others and show his superiority even if his manner of driving involves risks
He drives fast in order to show his abilities

correct_answers.text: He treats others like partners, drives calmly and cooly and refrains from showing that he is superior

comment: A good driver adheres to the traffic regulations and is characterized by a cooperative behavior in dealing with other road users. He/she refrains from risky driving styles and careless overtaking maneuvers. A good driver does not have to prove his/her skills to others.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: Travelling on a main road after a lengthy period of time of following behind, you are finally able to overtake a very slow-moving car. What should you do?

options.text: - I pull back in after an adequate distance in order not to impede the other driver
- I brake briefly in order to call the attention of the other driver to his slow speed
- I drive especially slowly in order to emphasise to the other driver the effects of his driving style

correct_answers.text: - I pull back in after an adequate distance in order not to impede the other driver

comment: You should stay calm in this situation and overtake with a sufficient safety distance without endangering other road users. Harassing others by tightly cutting them should be avoided. Otherwise an accident could occur.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: The vehicle ahead has prevented you from overtaking for some time now. What is the right course of action?

options.text: I wait until I am able to overtake
I close the gap
I sound my horn and flash my headlights persistently

correct_answers.text: I wait until I am able to overtake

comment: The car driver has to wait until overtaking is possible without danger and always maintain the necessary safety distance to the vehicle in front. Stay calm, because tailgating, turning the headlights on full beam for a long time or honking is considered coercion and will be punished with fines or even a withdrawal of your driving license.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: Right before you want to drive off, you got annoyed about something and have become very angry. What should you do?

options.text: I only drive off, once I have calmed down again
I drive off, in order to distract myself from my anger
I try to reach my destination quickly, so that I can calm down there

correct_answers.text: I only drive off, once I have calmed down again

comment: Getting into the car angrily can negatively affect your driving style. If you are angry, your driving style is also aggressive and limited. Therefore, only get into your vehicle when you're abreacted.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: You have just avoided a road traffic accident by performing an emergency braking manoeuvre. Your hands and knees are shaking. You are still far from your destination. What should you do?

options.text: - to the next stopping place, in order to calm myself down
- to my destination, so that I can recover my composure

correct_answers.text: - to the next stopping place, in order to calm myself down

comment: You should calm down first. Because your restlessness can have a negative effect on your driving style. Find a place to stop and relax. Afterwards you may continue the journey.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: What should you be aware of when driving a car after a long day's work?

options.text: I drive with a lower level of concentration
I will become tired more quickly
I make fewer driving errors

correct_answers.text: I drive with a lower level of concentration
I will become tired more quickly

comment: After a long day at work, you are usually not fully productive and get tired faster. That's why mistakes while driving can increase and your concentration decreases.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: How can you recognise a good driver?

options.text: - exhibits a calm and relaxed driving style
- refrains from responding to provocations on the road
- always informs other traffic participants of their driving errors

correct_answers.text: - exhibits a calm and relaxed driving style
- refrains from responding to provocations on the road

comment: A good driver always takes care to act in partnership and also knows that people can make mistakes.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: The [red] car in front of you has been driving slowly for some time now. What is the correct course of action in this situation?

options.text: I maintain my speed
I overtake, because the road is clear
I close the distance and sound my horn

correct_answers.text: I maintain my speed

comment:
You maintain your speed so as not to tailgate and keep the required safe distance. It is forbidden to tailgate, tailgate too closely or honk your horn in traffic.
The road is clear, but you can only see as far as the next bend. The visible distance is too short for an overtaking manoeuvre.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: What frequently causes young people to have “disco accidents”?

options.text: A lack of awareness of the road traffic
A high readiness to take risks
A defensive driving style

correct_answers.text: A lack of awareness of the road traffic
A high readiness to take risks

comment:
Young drivers in particular have less driving experience and a higher willingness to take risks through showing off. Dangerous situations are assessed more poorly and accidents occur more frequently.
A defensive driving style can prevent accidents.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: Why can driving under pressure of time be dangerous?

options.text: - risks are frequently underestimated
- the driver frequently goes too fast
- a defensive driving style is frequently adopted

correct_answers.text: - risks are frequently underestimated
- the driver frequently goes too fast

comment: When you are under time pressure, you may underestimate dangers because your willingness to take risks increases and people often drive too fast. You should still drive defensively and stick to the speed limits to avoid endangering yourself and others.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: You are on a road outside of a built-up area, and a car in front of you is driving much slower than is permitted to and has the capacity to. What is the right course of action?

options.text: I adjust my speed to that of the car
I overtake at a suitable place
I flash my headlights, until the car begins to drive faster

correct_answers.text: I adjust my speed to that of the car
I overtake at a suitable place

comment: Even if you don't like it, you must adapt your speed to that of the car and not get too close to it. Only overtake at a suitable place and not in front of it. Do not endanger yourself or others.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: Why is it not advisable to change lanes frequently?

options.text: Because this can increase the risk of driving errors
Because the time gained by this is generally very small
Because this can endanger other road users

correct_answers.text: Because this can increase the risk of driving errors
Because the time gained by this is generally very small
Because this can endanger other road users

comment: Every lane change requires certain activities: observing traffic, flashing, changing the lane yourself. In this case, other road users can be overlooked and endangered. Changing lanes often doesn't save you much time, but the more often you change lanes, the more likely you are to make mistakes.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: You have narrowly avoided a road traffic accident through emergency braking. Your hands and knees are shaking. What is the right course of action?

options.text: I take a break at the soonest possible opportunity, in order to calm myself
Later, I ponder if I could have avoided the situation
I continue driving in order to calm myself

correct_answers.text: I take a break at the soonest possible opportunity, in order to calm myself
Later, I ponder if I could have avoided the situation

comment:
Stop at the next opportunity and take a break until you have calmed down. Maybe you can get out, walk a few metres and take a deep breath. 
You should also go through the situation again in your head later, as you may realise what didn't go perfectly. That way you can adjust your driving behaviour in the future.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: While driving, you become very annoyed at the behaviour of another road user. What is the right course of action now?

options.text: I continue to concentrate on the road traffic
I continue driving in such a way that my anger does not negatively affect road safety
If necessary, I take a break to calm myself down

correct_answers.text: I continue to concentrate on the road traffic
I continue driving in such a way that my anger does not negatively affect road safety
If necessary, I take a break to calm myself down

comment: It is important that you are not distracted by the traffic if you are annoyed by the behaviour of other drivers, because road safety is paramount. Concentrate on the traffic and continue driving calmly; if you are emotionally agitated while driving, you could overlook dangers. If necessary, take a break and only continue driving when you have calmed down.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: Why does environment friendly driving in general have a beneficial effect on traffic safety?

options.text: Because drivers think ahead when travelling, so that possible dangers can be recognized in time and well avoided
Because environment friendly driving avoids high speeds so that dangerous situations occur less frequently
Because you can only drive slowly using alternative fuels

correct_answers.text: Because drivers think ahead when travelling, so that possible dangers can be recognized in time and well avoided
Because environment friendly driving avoids high speeds so that dangerous situations occur less frequently

comment: Avoid high speeds and drive anticipatory. This not only has a positive effect on the environment. It also contributes to greater road safety.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: The queue you are driving in is overtaken in an inconsiderate manner by a car. Because of oncoming traffic the driver wants to join the queue in front of the car driving in front of you. This driver is annoyed and "closes the gap". What do you do?

options.text: You give in and let the jostling driver join the queue
You also "close the gap" in order to teach the jostling driver a lesson
Nothing, since you are not concerned

correct_answers.text: You give in and let the jostling driver join the queue

comment: In such a situation, by deliberately giving in, you should reduce the speed and giving the other road user space to go back into lane in order to reduce the risk of an accident. Remember that everyone can misjudge.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: A truck indicating to the right is driving in front of you. An impatient car driver is jostling you. What can you do?

options.text: I only overtake when I am completely certain that the traffic situation allows overtaking without danger
I open up the distance to the truck to make overtaking easier for the jostling driver
I overtake because I assume that the truck driver wishes to signal to me that overtaking is possible

correct_answers.text: I only overtake when I am completely certain that the traffic situation allows overtaking without danger
I open up the distance to the truck to make overtaking easier for the jostling driver

comment: In this situation it is better to cut back and keep a safe distance. Maybe the truck driver would like to signal that the road is clear. However, it may also be that he/she intends to stop or turn right. Only overtake if there is no danger. Increase the distance to the truck so that the pushy driver can overtake.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: On a road not within a built-up area, a car is driving in front of you at a speed somewhat slower than that permitted. You are annoyed at the slower-moving car. What should you do?

options.text: I adjust my speed to that of the vehicle ahead
I overtake at a suitable place
I flash my headlights, until the car in front begins to drive faster

correct_answers.text: I adjust my speed to that of the vehicle ahead
I overtake at a suitable place

comment: You should definitely wait for a safe situation to overtake. Harassing someone by tailgating or flash light, however, represents a threat or even coercion. You should refrain from doing so.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: What can frequently lead to road traffic accidents during night-time recreational drives at the weekend?

options.text: - little experience driving after dark
- little experience with fully occupied vehicles
- little knowledge of road traffic regulations

correct_answers.text: - little experience driving after dark
- little experience with fully occupied vehicles

comment: Too little driving experience during the dark and a lack of knowledge about driving behavior in fully occupied vehicles often leads to accidents during nocturnal recreational rides on the weekend.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: You are under time pressure. What must you ensure?

options.text: - to exceed the speed
- to drive through the traffic lights even when red
- to reduce the safety

correct_answers.text: - to exceed the speed
- to drive through the traffic lights even when red
- to reduce the safety

comment: Even if you are under time pressure, you must follow the traffic rules. This also means that you comply with the speed limits. After all, excessive speed is THE main cause of accidents.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: Serious accidents frequently occur when young people drive cars during night-time recreational drives at weekends. What causes can be particularly relevant here?

options.text: Inappropriate speed
High risk readiness
Hesitant driving style

correct_answers.text: Inappropriate speed
High risk readiness

comment: Unreasonable speed and willingness to take risks often lead to serious accidents among young people during weekend rides at night.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: After overtaking you, a car pulls back into lane without leaving sufficient space in front of you. What should you do?

options.text: I remain calm in order to avoid conflicts
I brake in order to ensure that the safety distance is again established
I flash my headlights in order to call attention to the impediment

correct_answers.text: I remain calm in order to avoid conflicts
I brake in order to ensure that the safety distance is again established

comment: The car driver in the overtaking vehicle shows a misconduct that should not disturb you. Stay calm, do not honk and do not turn on the flash light. Decelerate slightly and restore the required safety distance between the vehicles.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: The risk of causing an accident when driving a vehicle is significantly higher for drivers aged between 18 and 24. What reasons are frequently relevant here?

options.text: Too little driving experience
Over-estimation of own capabilities
Higher levels of risk readiness

correct_answers.text: Too little driving experience
Over-estimation of own capabilities
Higher levels of risk readiness

comment: Young car drivers often have too little experience to be able to correctly assess road traffic risks. They often drive carelessly and riskily, overestimate their abilities and rely on the safety of the vehicles they control. By testing their car and their own driving skills, they sometimes get into unmanageable situations.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: While you are in a traffic jam, looking in your rear-view mirror you see a motorcyclist "snaking" past the stationary line of vehicles. What should you do?

options.text: I let him drive past
I sound my horn and note his registration
I take steps to ensure that he too must come to a stop

correct_answers.text: I let him drive past

comment: Under no circumstances should you act illegally just because another road user violates applicable rules. It is forbidden for you as a car driver to honk in this situation, to stop the motorcyclist or to let him pass.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: You are driving on a main road and a car following behind is "tailgating" you. How should you react?

options.text: I maintain my speed and keep to the right to enable the car following behind to overtake
I increase my speed until the car following behind ceases "tailgating" me
I reduce my speed until the car following behind ceases "tailgating" me

correct_answers.text: I maintain my speed and keep to the right to enable the car following behind to overtake

comment: When driving on a highway and being harassed by the car behind you, you should keep calm and control your speed at an appropriate pace. You should avoid slow driving so as not to hinder the flow of traffic. However, you should also not be tempted to drive faster. It's best to let the pushy driver pass at the next opportunity.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: You overtake on a motorway. Behind you a car approaches at high speed, with headlights and indicators flashing. What should you do?

options.text: I continue overtaking swiftly
I pull over into the right-hand lane as soon as possible
I gently decelerate

correct_answers.text: I continue overtaking swiftly
I pull over into the right-hand lane as soon as possible

comment: The only thing you can do is to keep calm! Stay calm and do not try to score off the pushy driver. It is best to let him pass. If you have sufficient overtaking speed, you can still complete the overtaking process. As soon as the next opportunity arises, you should switch to the right lane and let the pushy driver pass.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: Five young friends are driving in a car to a recreational event. The mood is exuberant. To what risks can this give rise?

options.text: - be distracted from events on the road
- be induced to drive in a risky manner
- be induced to drive slowly

correct_answers.text: - be distracted from events on the road
- be induced to drive in a risky manner

comment: For the car driver, there is a risk of getting carried away by the mood. He/She can be distracted by the others and overlook traffic hazards and make driving mistakes. It is recommended to set up rules of conduct for the passengers before starting the journey. So, the car driver is not a spoilsport or tempted in any way.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: While driving on the motorway you overtake several vehicles. A vehicle approaches you from behind with indicators and headlights flashing. What should you do?

options.text: I continue driving until I can again pull into the right-hand lane
I turn on my hazard lights briefly to urge the vehicle behind to keep its distance
I brake briefly to prompt the vehicle behind to keep its distance

correct_answers.text: I continue driving until I can again pull into the right-hand lane

comment: The dense, aggressive tailgating of the following vehicle endangers all road users. For this reason, you should try to change to the right-hand lane in compliance with the safety distance. Any braking maneuver would only worsen this dangerous situation. Switching on the hazard light is prohibited in this case.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: You want to overtake. Why should you not do so?

options.text: The oncoming traffic
The bend in the road
The state of the road surface

correct_answers.text: The oncoming traffic
The bend in the road

comment: A car driver may only overtake if he/she can see that the opposite lane is free. In this situation, the oncoming traffic cannot be seen, so you must not overtake.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: You were in a bad mood prior to commencing your journey. What consequences should you avoid when driving?

options.text: Distraction
Aggressiveness
Caution

correct_answers.text: Distraction
Aggressiveness

comment: Anything that could negatively affect your safe driving should be avoided. Besides distractions, this also includes aggressiveness. If you're upset, do not get behind the wheel immediately afterwards.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: Which is the stamp of a responsible driver?

options.text: He anticipates the mistakes of other road users
He avoids driving when tired
He is assertive towards other road traffic

correct_answers.text: He anticipates the mistakes of other road users
He avoids driving when tired

comment: A responsible car driver expects mistakes from other road users and does not sit behind the wheel while he/she is very tired or cannot control his/her feelings. Furthermore, he/she does not always insist on his right and cannot be distracted.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: What emotions can influence driving behaviour?

options.text: Happiness and exuberance
Worry and sorrow
Anger and rage

correct_answers.text: Happiness and exuberance
Worry and sorrow
Anger and rage

comment: Strong emotions such as anger, fear and sadness as well as joy and exuberance usually influence the driving behavior. They distract the car driver from the road and often lead to risky, aggressive or over-cautious driving. Only when you're calm and balanced you should participate in traffic.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: What indications mean you should interrupt your journey?

options.text: Yawning frequently
Difficulty keeping your eyes open
Difficulties staying in lane

correct_answers.text: Yawning frequently
Difficulty keeping your eyes open
Difficulties staying in lane

comment: Brief microsleep often causes devastating accidents. If you have to yawn frequently, can barely keep your eyes open, or have trouble keeping your lane, you should stop your journey and take a rest.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: Your passenger wants to discuss something with you during the journey. What should you do?

options.text: - my driving
- the discussion

correct_answers.text: - my driving

comment: You should not be distracted while driving. If your passenger wants to discuss with you, you should stop the journey.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: During the journey your passenger informs you that you are repeatedly tailgating. What should you do?

options.text: I take the passenger’s comments seriously
I maintain a greater distance
I ignore the passenger’s comments

correct_answers.text: I take the passenger’s comments seriously
I maintain a greater distance

comment: You should take the safety advice of passengers seriously. Keep a larger distance. Within built-up areas, the distance to the vehicle in front should be at least three car lengths or approx. 15 m. Outside built-up areas, you should follow the "two-second rule of thumb".

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: At a red light in a built-up area, another driver apparently wants to provoke you into a street race. What should you do?

options.text: I totally ignore this behaviour
I accept the challenge, but without exceeding 50 km/h
I get out and confront the driver

correct_answers.text: I totally ignore this behaviour

comment: Don't be provoked and stay calm. Since road races are strictly prohibited, you should not pay attention to this behavior.

chapter_name: Affective Emotional Behaviour In Road Traffic
question_text: What frequently causes young people to have “disco accidents”?

options.text: A lack of experience driving after dark
Little experience with fully occupied vehicles
A distraction caused by passengers

correct_answers.text: A lack of experience driving after dark
Little experience with fully occupied vehicles
A distraction caused by passengers

comment: Young drivers in particular have less experience driving at night with crowded vehicles. In addition, the risk of accidents increases due to distracting passengers.
